Both shape how you architect the feature.

whyWrong.B: Inverts the inference. Without citations enabled there is no citation channel, so an uncited answer says nothing about whether retrieval succeeded.
whyWrong.C: Citations do more than display: they give you machine-readable locations back into the sources, which is what makes a grounding claim checkable. And shorter chunks is a separate retrieval decision.
whyWrong.D: The incompatibility is real and is worth designing around, but it does not make citations unavailable — it means you choose one or the other for a given request. Not enabling them for that reason is a decision, and it leaves the team without any grounding signal.

questions.mindset: You cannot debug grounding you never asked for: enable citations deliberately, chunk per document, and treat 'no citations' as meaningful only once the channel exists.

questions.scenario: Brantley's adjudicator over 180,000 claims a night is now the largest line item in the claims platform's cloud bill. The team has three candidate changes and no appetite for a quality regression: routing simple claims to a smaller model, forcing structured output instead of prose-plus-regex, and turning on prompt caching for the shared policy prefix.
questions.stem: Which TWO statements about where these levers actually act are accurate? Choose TWO.

options.text: Prompt caching acts on input tokens: cached prefixes are read at a fraction of base input price while writes cost more than base input, so a large stable prefix reused across every request is the clearest win — provided the varying per-request content sits after the breakpoint, and breakpoint placement matters because there is a lookback window a growing conversation can push past.

Structured output acts on output tokens and on retry volume. By compiling the schema into a grammar, it removes the prose-and-post-processing path, so the model emits only the fields you consume — but it adds a system prompt describing the format, so input tokens rise slightly, changing `output_config.format` invalidates the prompt cache for that thread, and the first request with a new schema pays extra latency while the grammar compiles, with compiled grammars cached for 24 hours from last use.
Structured output makes cached prefixes unnecessary, because the compiled grammar constrains generation independently of how much input is resent.
Model routing and caching are interchangeable, because the per-request saving from moving a claim to a smaller tier is roughly the same as the saving from reading the shared prefix from cache.
Because prompt caching reads are so much cheaper than base input, caching makes the input side of this workload effectively free, so cost reduction should focus entirely on output length.

questions.explanation: Two accurate statements, and together they are the cost map for this workload. Caching acts on input tokens: cache writes cost more than base input, cache hits cost a fraction of it, and breakpoints themselves are free, so the saving scales with how large and how stable the shared prefix is. Placement is the whole game — with a varying suffix, put the breakpoint at the end of the static prefix rather than on the varying block, and remember the lookback window: if a growing conversation pushes the breakpoint 20 or more blocks past the last cache write, the lookback misses it. Structured output acts differently, on output tokens and on retry volume: compiling the schema into a grammar removes the prose-and-regex path so the model emits only the fields you consume. It is not free, though — it adds a system prompt describing the format so input tokens rise slightly, changing `output_config.format` invalidates the prompt cache for that thread, and the first request with a schema pays compilation latency with grammars cached for 24 hours from last use. Those interactions are why 'just turn caching on' is not a complete plan.

whyWrong.C: Grammar-constrained generation and prefix caching are unrelated mechanisms. One constrains what may be emitted; the other reduces the price of re-reading a shared prefix.
whyWrong.D: They act on different token categories with different magnitudes. Comparing them without measuring the workload's input-to-output ratio and prefix stability is guesswork, and routing also carries a quality risk that caching does not.
whyWrong.E: Cache reads are cheaper, not free, and the untouched suffix still bills at base input. A workload's cost is decided by its whole prefix and output profile, not by the cached portion alone.

questions.mindset: Caching discounts a stable prefix; structured output removes prose and repair — and each has a cost of its own that belongs in the same model.

questions.scenario: Brantley's policy answers are graded automatically by a Python script that asserts the response contains a specific clause reference, then by an LLM judge scoring coherence 1-5. The script-based metric has moved from 96% to 95.8% since last month's prompt change; the LLM judge average moved from 3.9 to 3.86.
questions.stem: What is the correct reading of these two movements?

options.text: Neither movement is established as a regression. The code-graded metric is deterministic and therefore trustworthy as a signal, but a 0.2-point move needs a paired comparison on the same cases and a look at which cases flipped, because a small deterministic delta can still be a real effect. The LLM-judge movement is inside the noise the team already measured — an 8-point spread on identical code means a 0.04-point change carries no information at all. Report the deterministic metric as directional evidence and either stop tracking the judge average or re-establish its noise floor before quoting it.
Both movements are regressions. The code metric proves quality dropped and the judge confirms it, so the prompt change should be reverted.
Neither metric matters for this decision. Grade every response with an LLM judge so the metric reflects real answer quality rather than the presence of a clause reference.
The LLM judge's movement is the more reliable signal, because a 1-5 scale captures quality that a clause-reference assertion cannot. The deterministic metric is too coarse to judge.

questions.explanation: The two metrics do not carry the same evidential weight, and conflating them is the mistake. A code-based grader is deterministic: rerun it on the identical response set and you get the identical number, so a 0.2-point move is a real observation about behaviour — but attributing it to the prompt change still needs a paired comparison over the same cases plus an inspection of which cases flipped, because the same aggregate can come from one bad case replacing one good one. The LLM judge is the opposite case: it is a noisy measurement, and the team has already quantified that noise at 8 points of spread on identical code, so a 0.04-point movement is roughly two hundred times smaller than the instrument's own variance and carries no information. The methodological point is that you compare a signal to the noise floor of the instrument that produced it, and you use the deterministic grader where you can, reserving the judge for what assertions cannot capture.

whyWrong.B: Treats the judge movement as confirmation when it is smaller than the judge's measured variance, and ignores that a deterministic delta needs case-level attribution before it is called a regression.
whyWrong.C: Inverting the strength of the instruments. Deterministic grading is the stronger signal precisely because it is reproducible; an LLM judge is for criteria assertions cannot express, not a replacement for them.
whyWrong.D: Has it backwards. A 1-5 scale is more expressive and far less reliable, which is why the docs suggest using a different model as judge and why repeated runs are needed before quoting its average.

questions.mindset: Judge a signal against its instrument's noise floor: deterministic graders move reproducibly and deserve case-level attribution, LLM-judge deltas smaller than its spread mean nothing.
